The Ferryman is richly absorbing, its plot kinked and ample, its writing generous — everyone gets a story, a joke and a speech that lets you glimpse their soul.
It is, like Jerusalem before it, an extraordinary, thrilling act of belief in the power of theatre to gather people in a room and make them listen.
The Ferryman has lived up to the faith already invested in it.
Jez Butterworth’s vast, sprawling superbly directed (by Sam Mendes) play really does fall into that rare category – unmissable.
The script is deliciously anecdotal, sparkling with humour and it succeeds at painting detailed portraits of well-rounded characters.
With acting like this, it's really an amazing experience, if a rather heartless one. But Butterworth's storytelling finesse carries all before it.

cn.t: Butterworth's epic family drama set during the Troubles earns widespread acclaim for its sprawling ambition, vivid characters, and theatrical vitality. Critics hail it as a magnificent, gripping work that justifies its considerable length.
